Boastful describes a person who talks about themselves — their achievements, possessions, abilities, or experiences — in an excessive, show-off way, usually to make others see them as impressive or superior. In plain terms, a boastful person loves to brag, and they do it often, even when nobody asked.

The key word here is excessive. It is not simply about being happy with yourself. It is about loudly and repeatedly advertising how great you are to others.
What a Boastful Person Actually Does

A boastful person does not just feel good about themselves on the inside. They feel a strong need to announce it. They will bring up their own success, talent, or belongings in conversations — sometimes even when it has nothing to do with what is being discussed. They often exaggerate to make themselves sound even more impressive. And they tend to keep doing it, again and again, without realising (or caring) that it bothers others.

For example:

  • Someone who got a promotion at work might mention it once, which is perfectly normal. But a boastful person will bring it up in every conversation, with every person they meet, for weeks.
  • A boastful student might constantly remind classmates how high their grades are, especially after a test.
  • A boastful traveller will turn every conversation into a story about all the expensive places they have visited.
The Feeling It Creates in Others

This is important: the word boastful carries a negative judgement. When we call someone boastful, we are saying their behaviour is annoying, tiresome, or off-putting. Listeners tend to feel:

  • Bored, because they have heard it too many times.
  • Uncomfortable, because it feels like the boastful person is trying to make them feel lesser.
  • Irritated, because the conversation always ends up being about the same person.

A boastful person, by talking about themselves so much, usually pushes other people away — even if that is the last thing they intend to do.

Most boastful people are driven by a deep desire to be admired or envied. They want others to look up to them. Sometimes this comes from insecurity — they brag because, deep down, they are not sure people value them, so they try to force the admiration by advertising their own greatness.

This, however, does not make the behaviour less annoying to those around them.

Not every boastful moment is equally extreme. Someone can be:

  • Mildly boastful — They occasionally slip into bragging, perhaps without even fully realising it. "Oh, I actually won that award three years in a row, but anyway..."
  • Very boastful — Every conversation circles back to how great, rich, talented, or successful they are. It is a dominant personality trait.

Context also matters. If someone asks you about your achievements, talking about them is not boastful. Boastfulness is specifically about unsolicited, repeated, self-congratulatory talk.
How Boastful Differs from Similar Words

This is where many learners get confused, so let us be precise.

Confident — A confident person believes in their own abilities. They do not need to tell others how good they are. Confidence is quiet and positive. Boastfulness is loud and negative.

Proud — Feeling proud is a natural, healthy emotion. You can feel proud of something without ever mentioning it to anyone. Pride lives inside you. Boastfulness is what happens when that feeling gets turned into excessive public performance.

Arrogant — An arrogant person believes they are better than others and acts as though others are beneath them. Arrogance is about attitude and how you treat people. Boastfulness is specifically about talking — it is about bragging. A person can be boastful without being arrogant, and arrogant without being boastful, though the two often go together.

Conceited — A conceited person has an inflated internal opinion of themselves. It is about what they believe in their own mind. Boastfulness is the external expression — the showing off. Conceit is the root; boastfulness is often the visible result.

Humble — A humble person does not draw attention to their own achievements. Even if they are talented or successful, they do not feel the need to advertise it. Humility is widely considered a virtue.

Modest — A modest person downplays their own achievements and abilities, even when praised. They are uncomfortable being the centre of attention for their own greatness.

Self-deprecating — This person goes even further. They make light of or gently make fun of their own flaws or mistakes. It is almost the complete opposite of boastful.

Unassuming — An unassuming person does not try to impress others. They carry themselves without any sense of wanting to show off.

• He was so boastful about his new car that everyone at the party quietly tried to avoid him.
  • She had genuine talent, but her boastful attitude made it hard for people to appreciate her.
  • His boastful remarks about his salary made his colleagues feel uncomfortable and disrespected.
  • The team captain was skilled but boastful, which created tension in the group.
  • Nobody liked working with him because he was boastful and never gave credit to others.
  • She tried not to sound boastful, but she could not help mentioning her award for the fifth time that evening.

If you need to remember just one thing about this word:

Boastful = talking too much about yourself to impress others, in a way that feels excessive and self-centred.

It is always used as a negative description. Nobody says "She is wonderfully boastful." It is a flaw — one that reveals a person's need for admiration and their lack of awareness about how they are affecting those around them.

When you call someone boastful, you are saying: "This person brags too much, and it is tiresome."
